title: How NetBeez Fits Into Daily Network Operations
summary: Build a daily network monitoring workflow with NetBeez: spot issues in Buzz, investigate evidence, run Ad Hoc tests, and verify improvements.
body_markdown:
Network monitoring is often associated with incidents. A user reports a slow application, an office loses connectivity, or voice calls begin to break up. The network team opens its tools and starts looking for the cause.


NetBeez is useful in those moments, but that is only part of its role. Its agents[continuously test from the places where users connect](https://netbeez.net/network-monitoring) , giving teams evidence before, during, and after an incident.


NetBeez NextGen organizes that work into a simple flow: see what needs attention, investigate the evidence, run additional tests when needed, and verify the result.


## **Start with Buzz**


Buzz is the home view in[NetBeez NextGen](https://netbeez.net/solution/) . It brings the status of sites, remote users, Wi-Fi networks, internet service providers, applications, and recent events into one place.


The example below shows why that broader view matters. The overall network experience status is Healthy, but Buzz still shows one unreachable site, three offline remote users, and a Wi-Fi network with 50% of its sensors at risk. The environment is not experiencing a general outage, but there are individual conditions that may deserve attention.


This allows an operator to begin with the full environment instead of opening individual agents and tests one at a time. The purpose is not to investigate every variation. It is to notice when a location, user group, network, or service behaves differently from the rest.


*Buzz brings network experience into one view. Despite an overall Healthy status, one site is unreachable and 50% of the Wi-Fi sensors are at risk.*


## **Follow the supporting evidence**


From Buzz, the operator can move into the relevant user, agent, target, or Wi-Fi network and review the measurements behind the summary.


In this Wi-Fi example, the left side shows alerts opening and closing for services tested by Agent A. The timeline aligns those alerts with signal strength, link quality, bit rate, and wireless access-point events over the same four-hour period.


That context is more useful than viewing an application warning or wireless metric by itself. The operator can see whether degraded application performance occurred near reconnect events or changes in wireless conditions, and then decide what to investigate next.


The view does not automatically prove that a reconnect caused the packet loss or that the access point is the root cause. It provides the timing and measurements needed to narrow the investigation without making an unsupported conclusion.


*Agent A shows Wi-Fi measurements alongside application packet-loss warnings. Access-point reconnect events provide timing context for the investigation.*


## **Run the next test from the affected agent**


Continuous monitoring establishes what changed and when. Sometimes the engineer still needs a new test to answer the next question.


NetBeez Ad Hoc testing makes it possible to run diagnostics from the relevant agent while the issue is happening. The available tests include ping, DNS, HTTP, traceroute, iPerf, network speed, VoIP, packet capture, and custom commands.


In the example below, the operator runs a DNS test from Agent A over its Wi-Fi interface. The test uses the agent’s default DNS server and sends five UDP queries to mail.google.com. All five complete successfully, with resolution times between 0.1 and 15 milliseconds.


This result confirms that DNS resolution worked from that agent at that moment. It does not prove that the intermittent Wi-Fi condition has disappeared, but it helps eliminate a persistent DNS failure and directs the investigation toward the remaining evidence.


That is the role of Ad Hoc testing in the workflow: use the continuous data to identify the problem, then run a focused test to confirm or eliminate a specific possibility.


*A completed DNS test from the affected Wi-Fi agent shows the destination, interface, UDP configuration, and the resolution time of every query.*


## **Verify what happened after taking action**


Troubleshooting should not end when a configuration is changed, an access point reconnects, or a provider says that a problem has been corrected.


Because NetBeez continues testing throughout the incident, the team can return to the same measurements and verify whether the alerts stopped, wireless conditions stabilized, and application performance recovered. The historical data also shows whether the improvement lasted or the condition returned later.


This closes an important gap in many incident workflows. Instead of relying only on a user saying that things seem better, the team has evidence showing how the experience changed before and after its action.


The same evidence can then support a help-desk update, engineering escalation, provider case, or internal report.


## **One workflow, used by different teams**


Not everyone needs the same level of detail. The service desk can use NetBeez to determine scope and prepare a better escalation. Network engineers can compare measurements and run additional tests. IT leaders can review recurring issues and see whether completed work produced measurable improvements.


The workflow remains the same:


1. Buzz shows what needs attention.
2. The operator follows the supporting evidence.
3. Ad Hoc testing answers the next diagnostic question.
4. The team takes action.
5. Continuous monitoring verifies the result.


That is how NetBeez becomes part of daily network operations rather than a tool opened only during difficult incidents.
